### A tap contains every mode at once {#sec-m3-tap}

Strike a beam and let go. What follows is free vibration: no forcing, only the
structure's own dynamics, decaying under whatever damping it has. A tap is
broadband — it excites every mode the structure has — so a single recording of
a single tap contains all of them, separated in frequency and waiting to be
read off a spectrum.

That is the whole appeal of a tap test. No shaker, no swept excitation, no
force transducer: an impulse and a sensor.

### Frequencies without dimensions {#sec-m3-frequencies}

For a uniform cantilever of length $L$, cross-section $A = bh$, second moment
$I = bh^3/12$, density $\rho$ and modulus $E$, Euler–Bernoulli theory gives

$$
f_n = \frac{\lambda_n^2}{2\pi L^2}\sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho A}}
$$ {#eq-m3-euler}

where the $\lambda_n$ are the roots of $\cos\lambda\cosh\lambda = -1$:

$$
\lambda_1 \approx 1.8751, \qquad
\lambda_2 \approx 4.6941, \qquad
\lambda_3 \approx 7.8548
$$ {#eq-m3-lambda}

::: {.callout-important}
## The ratios are the testable prediction

Every quantity in @eq-m3-euler except $\lambda_n$ is a property of *this*
beam — and this rig's dimensions are
[not decided yet](../../hardware/beam-rig.qmd). Taking the ratio of two modes
removes all of them at once:

$$
\frac{f_2}{f_1} = \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^2 \approx 6.267,
\qquad
\frac{f_3}{f_1} = \left(\frac{\lambda_3}{\lambda_1}\right)^2 \approx 17.548
$$ {#eq-m3-ratios}

No length, no thickness, no modulus, no density. These two numbers are a
prediction that a measurement can falsify **without knowing anything about the
beam**, and they are the central result of this experiment.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
When a measured ratio departs from @eq-m3-ratios, the theory is rarely what
failed. The usual culprits, in order of likelihood: the clamp is not the ideal
built-in boundary the derivation assumes, so the effective length is not the
free length; the beam is not uniform, because the gauges, their wiring and any
tip target are lumped masses; and shear deformation and rotary inertia, which
Euler–Bernoulli neglects, matter more for the higher modes than the first.
That last one has a sign: it pushes the higher modes *down* relative to the
prediction, so $f_3/f_1$ coming out low is the expected direction of error.
:::

### Damping, two ways {#sec-m3-damping}

**Logarithmic decrement**, from the time domain. For a lightly damped mode the
envelope decays exponentially, so successive peaks $x_i$ separated by $k$
cycles give

$$
\delta = \frac{1}{k}\ln\frac{x_i}{x_{i+k}},
\qquad
\zeta = \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{4\pi^2 + \delta^2}}
$$ {#eq-m3-logdec}

**Half-power bandwidth**, from the frequency domain. The width of the
resonance where the power has fallen to half its peak — amplitude to
$1/\sqrt{2}$ — gives

$$
\zeta = \frac{\Delta f_{-3\,\mathrm{dB}}}{2 f_n}
$$ {#eq-m3-halfpower}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The two should agree, and when they do not the disagreement is informative.
The half-power estimate is biased **high** when the record is short, because
the finite observation window broadens every peak whether it is damped or not:
a record of length $T$ cannot resolve a bandwidth narrower than about $1/T$,
so a lightly damped mode measured over too few cycles reports the window's
width instead of its own. The logarithmic decrement has the opposite
weakness — it needs the mode isolated from its neighbours, which means
filtering, and a filter that is too narrow imposes its own decay.

Closely spaced modes break both. So does damping that is not viscous: dry
friction in a clamp gives a decay that is linear in time rather than
exponential, which shows up as curvature in a plot of $\ln x_i$ against $i$
and is invisible in a single $\delta$ computed from two peaks.
:::

### Mass loading: the sensor changes the answer {#sec-m3-loading}

An accelerometer of mass $m$ at the tip lowers the first natural frequency,
because it adds mass without adding stiffness. Using the first mode's
effective mass at the tip, $m_\mathrm{eff} \approx 0.2427\,\rho A L$,

$$
\frac{f_1'}{f_1} = \sqrt{\frac{m_\mathrm{eff}}{m_\mathrm{eff} + m}}
$$ {#eq-m3-loading}

This is a systematic error the experimenter introduces by measuring. It cannot
be averaged away, and it is not visible in a single recording — a loaded beam
rings perfectly cleanly at the wrong frequency.

**The strain gauge is the way out.** A foil gauge bonded to the surface adds
no measurable mass, so it reports the beam's true frequency whether or not the
accelerometer is fitted. Recording both channels, with and without the
accelerometer, measures the loading directly:

$$
\frac{f_1'}{f_1}
= \frac{f_1\left(\text{strain, accelerometer fitted}\right)}
       {f_1\left(\text{strain, accelerometer removed}\right)}
$$ {#eq-m3-loading-measured}

and needs no knowledge of $m$, $\rho$, $A$ or $L$.

### What the sampling has to deliver {#sec-m3-sampling}

This is the first experiment on this site whose measurand is a *frequency*, so
the quality of the time axis enters directly.

- **Rate.** The third mode is about 17.5 times the first
  (@eq-m3-ratios), so a rate chosen for $f_1$ will alias $f_3$. Sample for the
  highest mode you intend to report, and filter or verify the rest.
- **Record length.** Frequency resolution is $1/T$. Resolving a half-power
  bandwidth of $2\zeta f_n$ needs $T \gg 1/(2\zeta f_n)$ — which for a lightly
  damped mode is many cycles.
- **Grid quality.** [S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd) measured this platform's
  timing residuals and [S2](../S2-daq-dynamic/index.qmd) turned them into a
  penalty in bits. A frequency estimated against the device's own `t_us` is as
  good as that grid; estimated against a nominal rate, it inherits the clock
  error S2 measured in ppm, which is a *scale factor on every frequency here*.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A decaying signal is not a stationary one

Everything in @sec-m3-damping assumes the mode decays. That is exactly what
makes a periodogram's peak width ambiguous: a decaying sinusoid has a genuinely
broadened line, and the broadening *is* the damping. Do not window the record
so aggressively that the decay is hidden, and do not extend it so far past the
decay that the analysis is fitting noise.
:::
